title: A rule for bad days
hook: the one-breath version of everything: Hillel teaches the whole Torah to a man standing on one foot
tomorrow: why did a tea master shake leaves onto a path just swept?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: draft two. Same words, new stone, and the first draft kept beside it. Today, the version for days when even draft two is too much.

Some days the alarm doesn't go off, the bus pulls away as you reach the stop, and the meeting goes sideways before lunch. On a day like that, a whole rule of life feels like a joke. The Talmud tells of a man who wanted things short too. Not Jewish, and thinking of converting, he came to the sage Shammai and said: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand.
screen: `THE BUS PULLS AWAY.` → `THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` → `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.`

segments.voice: So the man went to Hillel and asked the same thing. Hillel didn't laugh, and didn't refuse. He gave him one line: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. In the Talmud's telling, Hillel accepted him as a convert, and the story is kept to show Hillel's patience. Notice its two halves. The first is the one-foot version: one sentence that holds everything. Jewish teachers call a line like that a kelal, a principle the details hang from. In another source, Rabbi Akiva names the verse "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" a great principle of the Torah. The second half matters just as much: go and learn. The short version doesn't replace the long one. It's the long one, folded small enough to carry. A bad day asks for the impossible, like learning everything on one foot. A rule for bad days is your Hillel line: one sentence, said in one breath, that still holds the whole rule. Not a lower bar. The same rule, on one foot. And when the day turns, the commentary is waiting.
screen: `HILLEL GIVES ONE LINE.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` · `A KELAL: THE PRINCIPLE.` · `NOW GO AND LEARN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE RULE, ON ONE FOOT.`

segments.voice: Find one sentence that holds your whole rule, short enough to say on a single breath. Breathe in, and on the way out say it out loud, once. Then let the rest of the sit be the commentary: quiet, unhurried, nothing to add.
A rule for bad days: one sentence that holds the whole rule, said in one breath. Hillel's way: the whole thing, on one foot.
screen: `A RULE FOR BAD DAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the hard days: the one-breath rule, and the rest is commentary, waiting. Day 1699, on one foot.

screen: `DAY 1699 COUNTS.` → `YOUR RULE · 11 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID A TEA MASTER SHAKE LEAVES ONTO A SWEPT PATH?`

howItsDone: Hillel's answer to the man on one foot is told in the Talmud (Shabbat 31a), where it shows his patience. On a personal rule, a bad-day version is one sentence that holds the whole, said in one breath.
